adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லின்
தொகையறிந்த தூய்மை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Avaiyarindhu aaraaindhu solluka sollin
Thokaiyarindha thooimai yavar.
kurals.meaning: People of clean mind who know the whole range of words should first understand the assembly in front of them, and only then speak, weighing what they say.
kurals.elementary: You talk one way to your baby cousin, another way to your friends, and another way to your teacher. A good speaker first looks at who is listening, then picks the right words for them.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by making knowledge of the audience (avai, the assembly or council) a precondition of speech: avaiyarindhu (having known the assembly) comes before aaraaindhu (having deliberated) and solluka (let them speak). Parimelazhagar explains that assemblies are of three grades relative to the speaker, those superior, equal, and inferior in learning (mikkaar, oththaar, thaazhndhaar), and the rest of the chapter works through how to behave before each. Sollin thokai (the aggregate of words) is glossed in the commentarial tradition, and in Solomon Pappaiah’s modern paraphrase, as the three kinds of expressive word: direct (senjol), figurative (ilakkanai-chol), and suggestive (kurippu-chol). Thooimai (purity) is a moral term, not a stylistic one: the speaker must not use this command of language to deceive the hearers. The ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net texts print the first word as “அவையறிநது”, an evident typing slip; the sandhi-joined text “அவையறிந் தாராய்ந்து” confirms the reading அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who desireth to obtain a knowledge of the customs of different countries, and also the languages of different nations, and of the usages of different orders of men, knoweth at once all that is high and low.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells King Dhritarashtra that a wise man studies how different peoples and classes speak and behave, and so understands everyone from the highest to the lowest.
hinduism.tie_back: Knowing “the usages of different orders of men” is exactly the knowledge of the assembly that the Kural requires before a person speaks.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: A good match on knowing your audience, but Vidura is describing general worldly wisdom, not speech in a council.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Colossians that their speech should be gracious and carefully seasoned, so that they can give each person the answer that fits that person.
christianity.tie_back: “How ye ought to answer every man” is the Kural’s point: fit your words to the particular hearer.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close. Both call for careful, purified speech shaped to each listener.

islam.quote_or_event: “You should preach to the people according to their mental caliber so that they may not convey wrong things about Allah and His Messenger.”
islam.explanation: Ali ibn Abi Talib warned teachers to speak to people at the level they can understand, so that they do not misunderstand what they hear and then spread wrong ideas. Bukhari places it under the heading of choosing some people rather than others for certain teachings.
islam.tie_back: Ali’s rule, speak according to the listener’s capacity, is the Kural’s rule of knowing the assembly before you speak.
islam._accuracy_note: Nearly identical teaching. Bukhari records it as Ali’s saying, not as a hadith of the Prophet.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb praises a word that fits its setting. The Hebrew phrase behind “fitly” suggests a word spoken in the right circumstances.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker who first studies the assembly is trying to produce exactly this fitting word.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the ideal of the fitting word, but does not mention the audience directly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha explains that he teaches through skillful means (upaya), shaping his teaching with many kinds of explanations, parables, and stories to suit the different dispositions and capacities of the beings he addresses.
buddhism.explanation: Mahayana tradition holds that the Buddha adjusted how he taught to the understanding of each audience, while the truth being taught stayed the same.
buddhism.tie_back: Skillful means is the Buddhist form of the Kural’s rule: understand the listeners first, then choose your words.
buddhism.source: Saddharma-pundarika (Lotus Sutra), Chapter 2 ‘Skilfulness’, trans. H. Kern
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel of adapting speech to the audience. The Lotus Sutra’s context is spiritual teaching, not a royal council.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greek army rushes for the ships in Iliad Book 2, Odysseus goes through the camp. To every chieftain he speaks courteously and reasons with him, but to every common soldier he speaks sharply and orders him back to his place.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows Odysseus, the master speaker, instantly changing his manner of speech according to the rank of the person in front of him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus reads each audience before he speaks, which is the skill this kural asks for.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A clear case of adapting speech to the audience. However, Odysseus’s harshness to commoners is sharper than anything the Kural recommends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Rhetoric may be defined as the faculty of observing in any given case the available means of persuasion.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines rhetoric as the skill of seeing what will persuade in each particular case. In the same chapter he says that persuasion depends partly on putting the hearers into the right frame of mind.
philosophy.tie_back: “In any given case” captures the Kural’s demand to study this particular assembly before speaking.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches on attention to the situation, but Aristotle has no equivalent of the Kural’s moral requirement of purity (thooimai).

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
இடைதெரிந்து நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லின்
நடைதெரிந்த நன்மை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Idaitherindhu nankunarndhu solluka sollin
Nadaitherindha nanmai yavar.
kurals.meaning: Good people who know how words carry meaning should pick the right moment, understand the matter fully, and only then speak.
kurals.elementary: If you want to ask your mom for something, you don’t ask while she is rushing to catch a bus. You wait for a good moment and think it through first. Wise speakers wait for the right time too.
kurals.university: Where 711 stressed the audience, this kural stresses the moment: idai (interval, opening) is glossed by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as the court’s sevvi, its receptive moment, when the hearers are ready and willing to listen. Nankunarndhu (having understood well) requires full command of the matter, and Solomon Pappaiah adds that the speaker must avoid faults of both word and sense (sorkutram, porutkutram). Sollin nadai (the gait or course of words) refers to how each of the three kinds of word conveys its meaning, which parallels sollin thokai in 711. The parallel structure of 711 and 712 (sollin thokaiyarindha thooimaiyavar / sollin nadaitherindha nanmaiyavar) presents purity and goodness as twin moral qualities of the ideal counsellor. The text is the same in all sources consulted, apart from the sandhi joining (“சொல்லி னடைதெரிந்த”).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking truthfully and beneficially and in avoiding speech that offends.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna counts disciplined speech, meaning speech that is true, helpful, and does not upset the listener, as a form of spiritual austerity (tapas).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker, who waits for the right opening and speaks only what is fully understood, is practising this austerity of speech.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches on careful, beneficial speech, but the Gita says nothing about timing, which is the centre of this kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks that speech be measured by its effect on the hearers: it should build them up and do them good.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it keeps the listeners’ good in view when deciding what to say.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of speech that serves the hearers, but does not deal with choosing the right moment.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the Prophet to call people with wisdom (hikmah) and fine instruction. Commentators understand hikmah here as fitting the message to the hearers and the occasion.
islam.tie_back: Speaking “with wisdom” and “in a way that is best” is the Kural’s discerning, well-timed speech.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in spirit. The link to timing depends on the commentators’ reading of “wisdom”.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth teaches that every action has its proper season, including speech and silence.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s idai, the right opening for speech, is Koheleth’s “time to speak”.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on timing. Koheleth states it as a general law of seasons, not as advice for counsellors.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, and endearing & agreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Prince Abhaya that he says only what is true and beneficial, and that even then he chooses the proper time to say it.
buddhism.tie_back: “A sense of the proper time” is the Kural’s idaitherindhu, knowing the moment.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel. Both texts require true content and the right timing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Shipwrecked and naked, Odysseus meets the princess Nausicaa. He weighs whether to clasp her knees as a suppliant or to plead from a distance, and decides that gentle words spoken from where he stands suit the moment best.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer stops the action to show Odysseus judging what kind of approach the situation calls for before he says a word.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus reads the moment before speaking, as the Kural requires.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A good illustration of speech timed and fitted to the occasion. The setting is a private encounter, not a council.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They would be sure to ask him whether he knew ‘to whom’ he would give his medicines, and ‘when,’ and ‘how much.’”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that anyone who only knows speech techniques is like a man who knows drugs but does not know which patient to give them to, when, or in what dose. Real rhetoric, like real medicine, requires that knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: “To whom” and “when” are the Kural’s two demands: know the assembly and know the moment.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A strong conceptual match, made through an analogy with medicine.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
அவையறியார் சொல்லல்மேற் கொள்பவர் சொல்லின்
வகையறியார் வல்லதூஉம் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Avaiyariyaar sollalmer kolpavar sollin
Vakaiyariyaar valladhooum il.
kurals.meaning: Anyone who starts to speak without understanding the assembly does not know the kinds of words, and has no real ability at all.
kurals.elementary: Imagine telling a scary ghost story at a little kid’s birthday party. The story may be good, but you picked the wrong crowd, and now everyone is crying. Not knowing your listeners can spoil even good words.
kurals.university: This kural is the negative of 711. Avaiyariyaar (those who do not know the assembly) who take up speaking (sollal mer kolpavar) are thereby shown to be sollin vakaiyariyaar, ignorant of the kinds of words. Valladhooum il (they have no ability whatever) uses an alapedai, a lengthened vowel (thooum), for emphasis. Parimelazhagar’s point is that eloquence cannot be separated from knowledge of the audience. A speaker who misjudges the assembly proves thereby that he does not know how words work, however learned he may be. The sandhi text reads “சொல்லன்மேற் கொள்பவர்”, and “வல்லதூஉ மில்”, which divide into the same words as சொல்லல்மேற் and வல்லதூஉம் இல்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That worst of men who entereth a place uninvited, and talketh much without being asked, and reposeth trust on untrustworthy wights, is a fool.”
hinduism.explanation: In his list of the marks of a fool, Vidura includes the man who talks at length when no one has asked him.
hinduism.tie_back: Talking “without being asked”, without reading the room, is how the Kural’s avaiyariyaar give themselves away.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close. Both treat speaking without regard to the hearers as a sign of foolishness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that answering before you have listened brings shame on the speaker.
christianity.tie_back: Speaking before you understand the matter or the assembly is the folly the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: A good match on premature speech. It is about the matter under discussion more than the audience.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids acting or speaking on matters you do not know, and warns that a person will answer for how he used his faculties.
islam.tie_back: The speaker who does not know the assembly is acting without knowledge, which this verse forbids.
islam._accuracy_note: A general principle about knowledge. It does not specifically address audiences.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth contrasts the gracious speech of the wise with a fool’s talk, which ruins the fool himself.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker who misreads the assembly is undone by his own words, as the fool is here.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the self-defeating nature of ill-judged speech, but does not name the audience as the cause.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is not wise because one speaks much. He who is peaceable, friendly and fearless is called wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada separates wisdom from talkativeness: a lot of speech is no evidence of wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise denies real ability to the person who is eager to speak but does not understand the assembly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Only a partial match. It rejects talkativeness as wisdom but says nothing about reading an audience.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Greek assembly, Thersites, a man of disorderly words, rails at Agamemnon out of turn. Odysseus rebukes him and strikes him with the sceptre, and the assembled army laughs at him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Thersites as the model of someone who speaks without any sense of place, rank, or occasion, and who is shamed for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Thersites is the avaiyariyaar of this kural: he speaks without knowing the assembly and ends up with no standing at all.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A vivid match. Homer’s scene also involves class contempt, which the Kural does not share.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay on talkativeness, Plutarch describes the chatterer who bursts into every conversation regardless of the company, is ignored or laughed at, and finds that nobody believes or values what he says.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch argues that the habitual talker loses the very thing speech exists for, which is being heard and trusted.
philosophy.tie_back: Plutarch reaches the Kural’s verdict: whoever speaks without regard to the listeners has no real power of speech.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, De garrulitate (On Talkativeness), Moralia 502B-515A (trans. W. C. Helmbold)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in theme. Plutarch focuses on compulsive talking rather than misjudging a council.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
ஒளியார்முன் ஒள்ளிய ராதல் வெளியார்முன்
வான்சுதை வண்ணம் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oliyaarmun olliya raadhal veliyaarmun
Vaansudhai vannam kolal.
kurals.meaning: Among the brilliant, shine with your full learning; among the dull, take on the plain color of white plaster and keep your brilliance hidden.
kurals.elementary: With your older brother who loves science, you can talk about planets and black holes. With your little sister you just say “the moon is pretty tonight.” You are just as smart either way. You simply show only as much as your listener can use.
kurals.university: The kural depends on a pun: oliyaar (the luminous, the learned) is set against veliyaar (the blank or white, the empty-minded), and before the latter one should take on the colour of vaansudhai, pure white lime plaster. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read this as appearing unlearned before the unlearned. Solomon Pappaiah softens it to coming down to the hearers’ level so that they can follow, and Kalaignar keeps the stronger sense of appearing ignorant. Plaster is bright but has no lustre of its own, so the image suggests someone who covers his learning without losing his integrity. This is the key verse of the chapter’s three-way scheme (superior, equal, inferior assemblies), and it is the source of the modern Tamil proverbial advice to “be white lime before fools.” The text agrees in all sources; the sandhi text reads “ஒளியார்முன் னொள்ளிய ராதல்” and “வண்ணங் கொளல்”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Unless one be asked, one must not explain (anything) to anybody, nor (must one answer) a person who asks improperly; let a wise man, though he knows (the answer), behave among men as (if he were) an idiot.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the learned not to display knowledge unasked or to answer improper questioners, and to behave, when appropriate, as if he knew nothing.
hinduism.tie_back: “Behave … as if he were an idiot” is the Kural’s white plaster: the wise man hides his light among those who cannot receive it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A remarkably exact parallel to the second half of the kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes adapting himself to every kind of listener so as to reach them.
christianity.tie_back: Paul becoming “weak to the weak” is close to the Kural’s speaker who takes on plain white before the plain.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on adapting to the audience. Paul’s aim is to win converts, while the Kural’s concern is prudence and dignity.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We did not send any messenger except [speaking] in the language of his people to state clearly for them.”
islam.explanation: God sends each prophet to speak in his people’s own language, so that the message will be clear to them.
islam.tie_back: Speaking at the level and in the idiom of your hearers is the Kural’s advice to take on their colour.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the principle of accommodation, but not the Kural’s idea of hiding one’s brilliance.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the introduction to the Guide for the Perplexed, Maimonides explains that he will present deep matters in scattered hints, so that they reach the prepared reader while remaining hidden from the unprepared multitude. He cites the rabbinic rule that such matters are to be taught only to those fit to receive them.
judaism.explanation: Maimonides deliberately veils his learning when speaking to people who are not ready for it, while revealing it to the qualified.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double rule: shine before the learned, and wear a plain surface before others.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, Introduction (trans. M. Friedländer)
judaism._accuracy_note: A close structural parallel. Maimonides concerns esoteric theology rather than everyday court speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Dhammapada commentary, the Buddha travelled to Alavi to teach a poor farmer. The man arrived exhausted and hungry after searching for a lost ox, so the Buddha had him fed before saying a word of Dhamma.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha set aside his teaching until he had met the listener’s actual condition, and remarked that hunger is the greatest of illnesses (Dhammapada 203).
buddhism.tie_back: Adjusting what you say and when you say it to where the listener actually is follows the Kural’s advice.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 203 (story of a lay disciple at Alavi)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Illustrates adapting to the hearer, but not hiding one’s learning. It is a commentarial story, not canonical text.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus returns to his own palace disguised by Athena as a ragged beggar. He hides his identity and cleverness among the insolent suitors, and reveals himself only when the moment and the company are right.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest mind among the Greeks chooses to look like nothing among people who would only abuse what he is.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus in rags is the Kural’s white plaster: brilliance deliberately covered before the unworthy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A good image of concealed brilliance, though Odysseus’s motive is strategy and revenge, not courtesy to the audience.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that uneducated speakers are often more persuasive than educated ones before popular audiences, because they argue from familiar, concrete things. He advises speakers to argue from what the hearers already accept, not from far-fetched premises.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sees that sophistication can work against a speaker before a plain audience, and that the effective speaker comes down to the hearers’ level.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the practical logic behind the Kural’s advice to put aside brilliance before the unlearned.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Closely related advice on adapting to plain audiences. It is paraphrased here, since the exact wording was not checked against a live source.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
நன்றென்ற வற்றுள்ளும் நன்றே முதுவருள்
முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nandrendra vatrullum nandre mudhuvarul
Mundhu kilavaach cherivu.
kurals.meaning: Of all the things called good, the best is the self-restraint that does not rush to speak first among elders who are wiser than oneself.
kurals.elementary: When your grandparents and their friends are talking about the old days, you might know a fun fact too. But the polite and smart thing is to listen first and let them speak. Waiting your turn shows you are growing up.
kurals.university: Mudhuvar are elders in knowledge, not just in age. In Parimelazhagar’s scheme this is the conduct suited to an assembly superior to oneself, just as 714’s first half suits an equal one. Mundhu kilavaa means not uttering (kila, to speak) first, not jumping ahead. Cherivu (literally density or closeness) here means self-restraint, what Mu. Varadarasanar calls adakkam, and it links this chapter to ch. 13, Adakkamudaimai. The superlative nandrendravatrullum nandre (good even among the things called good) is strong praise: such restraint is ranked above other virtues of the counsellor. Kalaignar’s paraphrase adds a vivid Tamil idiom, “like a cashew seed” (mundhiri kottai), for a person who pushes forward to speak. The text agrees across sources; the sandhi text reads “நன்றென்ற வற்றுள்ளு நன்றே முதுவருண்”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For the vital airs of a young man mount upwards to leave his body when an elder approaches; but by rising to meet him and saluting he recovers them.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that deference to elders is basic to right conduct, so much so that failing to show it is pictured as losing one’s life-breath.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s restraint before elders, letting them speak first, comes from the same culture of respect for seniors.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the principle of deference to elders, but concerns greeting, not speaking in council.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
christianity.explanation: James tells believers to put listening first and to be slow to speak.
christianity.tie_back: “Slow to speak” is the Kural’s mundhu kilavaa, not rushing to speak first.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in spirit. James addresses everyone, not specifically a junior among elders.

islam.quote_or_event: “I wanted to say that it was the datepalm tree but as I was the youngest of all (of them) I kept quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet asked his companions a riddle. Young Ibn Umar knew the answer but stayed silent out of deference to the senior companions present.
islam.tie_back: Ibn Umar’s silence is almost a dramatization of this kural: knowing, yet not speaking first among elders.
islam._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel. Other narrations add that Umar later wished his son had spoken, which qualifies the lesson.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise man does not speak before one who is greater than he in wisdom, And does not break into his fellow’s speech; And is not hasty to answer.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah lists seven marks of the wise, and the first is not speaking before someone greater in wisdom.
judaism.tie_back: This is virtually the Kural’s wording: do not speak first before those greater in learning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Tittira Jataka, a partridge, a monkey, and an elephant work out which of them is the eldest so that they can honour him. The Buddha tells the story when senior monks are left without lodging because younger monks took it first, and he rules that respect and precedence go to seniority.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha makes deference to elders a rule of the monastic community.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s restraint before elders applies the same principle of precedence to speech in council.
buddhism.source: Tittira Jataka (Jataka No. 37), in The Jataka, vol. 1, ed. E. B. Cowell
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the deference to seniors. The Jataka concerns lodging and honour, not speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arriving at Pylos, the young Telemachus hesitates to approach the aged king Nestor. He tells Athena, disguised as Mentor, that a young man is shy of questioning an elder.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Telemachus’s reluctance to speak first before a revered elder as proper modesty, and Athena encourages him gently.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Telemachus’s restraint before Nestor is the Kural’s modesty among elders.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A good match. Telemachus does in the end speak, at Athena’s urging.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In all cases, then, silence is a safe adornment for the young man, and especially so, when in listening to another he does not get excited or bawl out every minute, but even if the remarks be none too agreeable, puts up with them, and waits for the speaker to pause …”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch advises a young man attending a philosopher's lecture to listen in silence, to wait until the speaker has finished, and not to rush in with objections, recalling the saying that nature gave us two ears and one tongue.
philosophy.tie_back: Plutarch, like the Kural, praises the restraint of a younger person who does not hurry to speak before those wiser than himself.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On Listening to Lectures (De auditu), ch. 4 (tr. F. C. Babbitt)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Babbitt, Loeb Moralia vol. I, 1927). Strong match on a young person's restraint in speech before a more learned speaker; the Kural's ranking of this restraint as the best of all goods is not paralleled.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந் தற்றே வியன்புலம்
ஏற்றுணர்வார் முன்னர் இழுக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatrin nilaithalarndh thatre viyanpulam
Etrunarvaar munnar izhukku.
kurals.meaning: To slip up in speech before people who have taken in and understood vast fields of learning is like losing your footing and falling from the path.
kurals.elementary: A spelling mistake in a note to your friend is no big deal. The same mistake in the final round of a spelling bee, in front of the judges, feels like tripping on stage. Mistakes count most in front of experts.
kurals.university: Viyanpulam (wide fields, meaning vast areas of learning) etrunarvaar (those who have received and understood them) are the most demanding audience there is, and an izhukku (slip or lapse) before them is compared to aatrin nilaithalarndhatru, losing one’s footing on the way. Commentators disagree about aaru. Parimelazhagar and most modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) take it as the path of right conduct, so a verbal slip before the learned is as disgraceful as a good man’s moral lapse. Puliyur Kesikan takes aaru as a river and reads the image as a swimmer losing his footing mid-stream, so the lapse is dangerous and hard to recover from. The kural thus explains why 715’s restraint matters: before the learned the cost of error is very high. The text agrees in all sources; the sandhi text reads “ஆற்றி னிலைதளர்ந் தற்றே வியன்புல மேற்றுணர்வார் முன்ன ரிழுக்கு”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At King Janaka’s sacrifice, the boy-sage Ashtavakra challenges Bandin, the court debater who had defeated and drowned many scholars. In the debate before the learned assembly Ashtavakra wins, and Bandin, now silenced, meets the same fate he had imposed on others.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata tells how a famous debater’s failure before an assembly of the learned brought his complete downfall.
hinduism.tie_back: Bandin’s fall is the Kural’s image made literal: a slip before the learned is a fatal loss of footing.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Sections 132-134 (story of Ashtavakra), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Dramatic parallel of failure before a learned court. The story is about formal debate, not a counsellor’s verbal slip.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.”
christianity.explanation: James treats stumbling in speech as the hardest failing to avoid, and calls the person who never slips in word perfect.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s izhukku, a slip of speech, is the stumbling James speaks of.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the gravity of slips in speech, but without the Kural’s focus on a learned audience.

islam.quote_or_event: “A slave of Allah may utter a word without thinking whether it is right or wrong, he may slip down in the Fire as far away a distance equal to that between the east.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that one careless word can make a person slip and fall a great distance.
islam.tie_back: The hadith uses the same picture of a verbal slip as a fall, as the Kural does.
islam._accuracy_note: Striking match of the slip-and-fall image. The hadith’s stakes are eschatological, while the Kural’s are social.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To slip upon a pavement is better than to slip with the tongue: so the fall of the wicked shall come speedily.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira compares a slip of the tongue with a physical fall, and judges the verbal one worse.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s own comparison, a verbal slip likened to losing one’s footing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close image. Ben Sira belongs to Jewish wisdom literature and is quoted in the Talmud, but is outside the Hebrew canon.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Saccaka, a famous debater, boasts that he can make the Buddha tremble. In front of a large assembly of Licchavis he is refuted, and then sits silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head bowed, unable to reply.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows how a proud speaker’s reputation collapses at once when he stumbles before a discerning audience.
buddhism.tie_back: Saccaka’s humiliation is the Kural’s izhukku before the learned, a public loss of footing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good dramatic parallel. The setting is a debate, not a counsellor’s address.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Thracian singer Thamyris boasted that he could out-sing the Muses themselves. In the contest he failed before them, and they maimed him and took away his gift of song.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s brief story shows how overreaching before the greatest masters of an art ends in disgrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Failing before the Muses, the ultimate learned audience, is the Kural’s slip before those of vast learning.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The punishment is for arrogance as much as for error, so the parallel is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes questioning men with a reputation for wisdom, first politicians, then poets and craftsmen, and exposing, often in front of listeners, that they did not know what they claimed to know. This earned him their lasting resentment.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows how damaging it is to have one’s claim to knowledge fail under the questioning of someone more discerning.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates’ targets suffered what the Kural warns of: a lapse exposed before a keen examiner.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A related theme of exposure before the wise. Plato’s point is about ignorance of one’s ignorance, not court speech.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
கற்றறிந்தார் கல்வி விளங்கும் கசடறச்
சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Katrarindhaar kalvi vilangum kasadarach
Soltheridhal vallaar akaththu.
kurals.meaning: The learning of those who have studied deeply shines most brightly among people who can judge words flawlessly.
kurals.elementary: A great chess move looks like nothing special to someone who doesn’t know chess. Show it to a chess champion and they gasp, “Wow!” Your best work shines most in front of people who can understand it.
kurals.university: Vilangum (will shine, become manifest) is the key verb. Learning does not show its worth in a vacuum. It becomes visible only in the akam (midst, company) of those who are kasadara soltheridhal vallaar, able to examine words kasadara, without flaw or dross. Kasadu (impurity, dross) links back to Valluvar’s famous command in ch. 40, Kalvi (kural 391): “கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை.” There is a pairing here: flawless study (391) meets flawless hearing (717). Commentators note that this kural balances 716. The expert audience that punishes a slip is also the only audience that can properly recognise real learning. The ytamizh/thirukkural.net text “சொல்தெரிதல்” and the sandhi form “சொற்றெரிதல்” are the same word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Janaka offers a thousand cows with gold on their horns to the most learned of the Brahmins at his sacrifice. Yajnavalkya claims them, and his learning is tested one after another by the finest scholars of the court, including Asvala, Artabhaga, Uddalaka and Gargi. His answers stand, and the assembly acknowledges his mastery.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad shows a sage’s learning fully displayed only when it is tested by a court of equally learned questioners.
hinduism.tie_back: Yajnavalkya’s learning shines because his hearers can judge flawlessly, which is exactly what the Kural says.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Book 3 (trans. F. Max Müller)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A close narrative parallel of learning shown before a learned assembly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.”
christianity.explanation: The twelve-year-old Jesus sits among the teachers in the Temple, listening and asking questions, and those learned men are amazed by his understanding.
christianity.tie_back: His wisdom shows most clearly among the doctors of the law, hearers able to recognise it, as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: A good illustration of learning recognised by the learned. Luke’s purpose is Christological.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Are those who know equal to those who do not know?’ Only they will remember [who are] people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asserts the difference between the knowing and the unknowing, and says only people of understanding will take the lesson to heart.
islam.tie_back: Only “people of understanding” can take in what is said, just as the Kural says learning shines only before skilled judges.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that understanding requires capable hearers. The context is religious remembrance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud (Taanit 7a) applies this verse to Torah scholars, who sharpen each other in study. Learning grows keen among peers able to test it.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s learning that shines among skilled judges of words is the rabbinic picture of scholars sharpening scholars.
judaism.source: Proverbs 27:17 (KJV), as applied in Babylonian Talmud Taanit 7a
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong through the Talmudic reading. The verse itself concerns friends in general.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Before their famous dialogue, the monk Nagasena tells King Milinda that he will discuss only if the king talks as scholars do, where each side is corrected without anger, and not as kings do, who punish anyone who contradicts them. The king agrees, and the dialogue that follows shows Nagasena’s learning at its best.
buddhism.explanation: The Milindapanha makes a discerning, fair-minded partner the condition for real learning to appear.
buddhism.tie_back: Nagasena’s insistence on a “scholar’s” hearing is the Kural’s point: learning shines only before those able to judge words well.
buddhism.source: Milindapanha, Book 2, ch. 1 (trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, The Questions of King Milinda)
buddhism._accuracy_note: A close parallel on the right kind of audience for learned discourse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the court of the Phaeacians, Odysseus tells the story of his wanderings. King Alcinous praises him for telling his tale with the skill of a bard, and the whole hall sits spellbound.
greek_mythology.explanation: Among refined and discerning hosts, Odysseus’s wisdom and eloquence are fully recognised.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus’s gifts shine among hearers able to value them, as the Kural says learning does.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A good illustration. The Phaeacians are admiring hosts rather than critical examiners.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Seventh Letter, Plato writes that real understanding cannot be handed over like other subjects. It flashes out suddenly, like light kindled from a leaping spark, only after long shared inquiry and friendly questioning between capable minds.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that insight shows itself only in the company of fit fellow-inquirers.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s vilangum (shines forth) matches Plato’s image of learning lit up among worthy interlocutors.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on learning revealed through capable company. The letter’s authenticity is debated.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
உணர்வ துடையார்முன் சொல்லல் வளர்வதன்
பாத்தியுள் நீர்சொரிந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Unarva thudaiyaarmun sollal valarvadhan
Paaththiyul neersorindh thatru.
kurals.meaning: Speaking before people who can understand is like pouring water into a garden bed where plants are already growing.
kurals.elementary: Watering a plant that is already sprouting makes it shoot up fast. Watering an empty patch of dirt does nothing. Telling good ideas to someone who wants to learn is like watering the sprout.
kurals.university: This kural is the positive counterpart of the chapter’s closing image (720). Unarvadhu udaiyaar are people who have understanding, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah stress that they understand for themselves (thaame unargindra), even without being told. Speaking to them is like watering (neer sorindhatru) a paaththi, a small irrigated garden bed, in which the crop is valarvadhu, already growing of its own accord. The image is agricultural and exact: the water does not create growth but speeds up growth that is already under way, so the speaker’s words bear fruit at once. Parimelazhagar takes this as the assembly of equals in learning, and so completes the scheme begun in 714. The text agrees across sources; the sandhi text reads “உணர்வ துடையார்முற் சொல்லல்” and “பாத்தியு ணீர்சொரிந் தற்று”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mundaka Upanishad teaches that when a student has approached the teacher properly, with a calm mind and controlled senses, the wise teacher should fully impart to him the knowledge of Brahman, by which the imperishable is known.
hinduism.explanation: Teaching is to be poured out fully on the prepared and receptive student.
hinduism.tie_back: The prepared student is the Kural’s growing crop, and the teacher’s words are the water that makes it flourish.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on the receptive hearer. The Upanishad does not use the watering image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the sower, the word bears fruit only in the hearer who understands, the good soil.
christianity.tie_back: The same agricultural logic as the Kural: words bear fruit in understanding hearers.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close, image and meaning alike, though Jesus uses seed where Valluvar uses water.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me is like abundant rain falling on the earth, some of which was fertile soil that absorbed rain water and brought forth vegetation and grass in abundance.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares his teaching to rain. Fertile ground absorbs it and flourishes, while barren ground gains nothing.
islam.tie_back: The receptive soil that turns rain into growth is the Kural’s bed of growing crops.
islam._accuracy_note: An almost exact parallel of image and meaning.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah rules that the most profound teachings, such as the Work of the Chariot, may be expounded only to a student who is wise and understands on his own.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition keeps its deepest instruction for hearers who already have the understanding to take it further for themselves.
judaism.tie_back: “Understands on his own” is almost exactly the Kural’s unarvadhu udaiyaar, those whose understanding already grows by itself.
judaism.source: Mishnah Chagigah 2:1 (Sefaria, William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: A precise match on the kind of hearer. The Mishnah is restricting esoteric teaching rather than praising ordinary speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the parable of the plants, one great cloud rains equally on all the herbs, shrubs and trees of the earth. Each takes up the water according to its own nature and size and grows accordingly, and in the same way beings receive the Buddha’s single teaching according to their capacity.
buddhism.explanation: The Lotus Sutra pictures teaching as rain whose effect depends on how far each plant has grown.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s water poured on growing crops is the Lotus Sutra’s rain on plants that are ready to take it in.
buddhism.source: Saddharma-pundarika (Lotus Sutra), Chapter 5 ‘On Plants’, trans. H. Kern
buddhism._accuracy_note: A very close image. The Lotus Sutra stresses the rain falling on all equally, whereas the Kural focuses on the ready bed.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athena, disguised as Mentor, counsels the young Telemachus. Because he is ready to listen, her advice quickly takes root: he calls an assembly, sets sail to seek news of his father, and grows into a man fit to stand beside Odysseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess’s words fall on a mind already beginning to mature, and they produce rapid growth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Telemachus is the growing crop, and Athena’s counsel is the water that makes it flourish.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An illustrative narrative match only. Homer uses no agricultural image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says the true teacher, like a sensible farmer, chooses a fitting soul and plants in it words joined with knowledge. Such words can defend themselves and bear seed that grows again in other minds.
philosophy.explanation: Plato contrasts this real cultivation of receptive minds with scattering words carelessly, as in writing or in pleasure-gardens that come to nothing.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s farmer sowing in a fit soul is the Kural’s watering of the growing bed.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A strong parallel in both image and thought. It is paraphrased here because the passage was not re-verified verbatim.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
புல்லவையுள் பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க நல்லவையுள்
நன்கு செலச்சொல்லு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pullavaiyul pochchaandhum sollarka nallavaiyul
Nanku selach chollu vaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who can speak good things persuasively in a worthy assembly should never, even by forgetting themselves, speak them in a mean one.
kurals.elementary: You wouldn’t show your best drawing to kids who you know will just scribble on it and laugh. Save it for people who will really look at it. Good words should be shared with good listeners.
kurals.university: Pullavai (a low or mean assembly, from pul, grass, meaning petty or base) is set against nallavai (a good assembly). Pochchaandhum (even through forgetfulness) uses the root of ch. 54, Pochchaavaamai (Unforgetfulness): the speaker is not to slip, even for a moment, into speaking before an unworthy audience. Nanku sela sollu (to speak so that it goes in well) describes speech that enters and settles in the hearers’ minds. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as speech that is “fixed in the mind” (manadhil padhiyumaaru). The ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net texts print “நன்குசலச்”, apparently a corruption. The sandhi text “நன்கு செலச்சொல்லு வார்” and P. A. Muthukrishnan’s musical setting (“நன்கு செலச் சொல்லுவார்”, quoted on thirukkural.net) support the reading செல, which Parimelazhagar’s gloss (to cause to enter) also requires.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “This confidential knowledge may not be explained to those who are not austere, or devoted, or engaged in devotional service, nor to one who is envious of Me.”
hinduism.explanation: At the end of the Gita, Krishna forbids Arjuna to pass on its teaching to the undisciplined, the uninterested, or the hostile.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna’s ban on teaching the unfit hearer is the Kural’s refusal to speak in the pullavai.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.67 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A close parallel. The Gita concerns sacred teaching, not council speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words, when ye depart out of that house or city, shake off the dust of your feet.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells the disciples not to keep pressing their message on those who refuse to hear it, but to move on.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it advises withholding speech from an unreceptive audience.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches on leaving the unreceptive alone. The disciples do try once, whereas the Kural advises not speaking at all.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they hear ill speech, they turn away from it and say, ‘For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace will be upon you; we seek not the ignorant.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises believers who withdraw courteously from vain and hostile talk instead of engaging with it.
islam.tie_back: “We seek not the ignorant” is the Kural’s refusal to hold forth in the mean assembly.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on withdrawing from unworthy company. The verse is about ill speech, not wasted wisdom.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb warns that engaging a fool on his own terms lowers the wise to his level.
judaism.tie_back: Speaking in the pullavai risks this lowering, which is why the Kural forbids it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit. Proverbs 26:5 gives the opposite advice, and the pair is famously paradoxical.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the wanderer Vacchagotta asks the Buddha whether there is a self or not, the Buddha stays silent. He later explains to Ananda that either answer would only have confused Vacchagotta further or confirmed a wrong view.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha holds back even true teaching when the listener is not in a state to receive it properly.
buddhism.tie_back: His silence before an unready hearer is the Kural’s rule: do not speak good words where they cannot take root.
buddhism.source: Ananda Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 44.10 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: A parallel of skilful silence. Vacchagotta is confused rather than base, so the ‘mean assembly’ element is missing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a cock scratching for food finds a precious jewel. He says that it may be valuable to someone who prizes it, but he would rather have a single grain of barley.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable shows a treasure wasted on a finder who cannot value it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Good words spoken in a mean assembly are the jewel before the cock, a treasure the hearers will not value.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Cock and the Jewel’ (trans. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A close image of worth wasted on the unappreciative. Aesop is Greek fable rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never call yourself a philosopher, nor talk a great deal among the unlearned about theorems, but act conformably to them. … Thus, therefore, do you likewise not show theorems to the unlearned, but the actions produced by them after they have been digested.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the student not to lay out philosophical principles before people who cannot receive them, but to keep silent among them and show the fruit of those principles in conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts hold that worthy teaching should not be spoken before an audience unfit to receive it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter translation). Strong match on not speaking good things to an unfit audience. Epictetus' reasons are humility and the risk of speaking undigested doctrine, rather than the unworthiness of the assembly as such.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

kurals.tamil:
அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்தற்றால் தங்கணத்தார்
அல்லார்முன் கோட்டி கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Anganaththul ukka amizhdhatraal thanganaththaar
Allaarmun kotti kolal.
kurals.meaning: Holding forth before people who are not of one’s own kind is like nectar spilled into a gutter.
kurals.elementary: Imagine pouring the most delicious juice in the world down the drain. What a waste! Explaining something wonderful to people who don’t care at all is like that. The juice was good; it just went to the wrong place.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with its most memorable image. Amizhdhu (amrita, the nectar of immortality) is ukka (spilled) into an anganam, the drain of a house’s open courtyard: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss it as an unclean courtyard, Solomon Pappaiah as a sewer. Thanganaththaar allaar are those who are not of one’s own gana (group, circle), meaning not one’s equals in learning and outlook. Kotti kolal (to hold a discourse) uses kotti, cognate with Sanskrit goshthi (assembly, learned conversation). The simile, like 718’s, is exact. Nectar is not spoiled by being spilled, but it can never be recovered or drunk, so it is wasted. The sources differ slightly on one form: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read தங்கணத்தார், while the sandhi-joined text reads “தங்கணத்த ரல்லார்முற்” (தங்கணத்தர்). The meaning is unaffected.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even in times of dire distress a teacher of the Veda should rather die with his knowledge than sow it in barren soil.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the teacher that it is better to take his learning to the grave than to waste it on unfit recipients. The verse before it compares such teaching to good seed thrown on barren land.
hinduism.tie_back: Seed in barren soil and nectar in the gutter are the same waste: precious knowledge poured where it cannot be received.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A very close parallel in thought and in its image of waste. Manu’s wording is far more severe.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns against offering sacred things to those who will only trample them, and may turn on the giver.
christianity.tie_back: Pearls before swine and nectar in the gutter are twin images of treasure wasted on the unworthy.
christianity._accuracy_note: An almost identical teaching and image. Matthew adds the danger of retaliation.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts at what hears nothing but calls and cries … deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not understand.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an likens preaching to those who will not understand to a herdsman shouting at animals that hear only noise.
islam.tie_back: Words wasted on hearers who cannot take them in are the Kural’s spilled nectar.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches on speech wasted on the unreceptive. The Qur’an’s context is disbelief, not social rank or learning.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb forbids speaking wisdom to a fool, who will only scorn it.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s conclusion in plain words: wisdom poured before the wrong hearers is wasted.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Just after his awakening, the Buddha at first hesitates to teach. He reflects that the Dhamma is deep and subtle, and that a generation delighting in attachment would not understand it, which would only weary him. He agrees to teach only when he sees that some beings have little dust in their eyes.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha weighs whether his teaching would simply be wasted on listeners unable to receive it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s hesitation is the Kural’s worry about pouring nectar where it will be lost.
buddhism.source: Ayacana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 6.1 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: A close concern with wasted teaching. The Buddha’s compassion finally overrides it, whereas the Kural’s counsel stands.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra, given true prophecy by Apollo but cursed never to be believed, foretells the murder of Agamemnon and her own death. The elders of Argos listen, but they cannot grasp or accept her words.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her true and precious speech falls on hearers who cannot receive it, and it is completely lost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Cassandra’s wasted prophecy is nectar spilled into the gutter, the Kural’s picture of words lost on the wrong audience.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An evocative match of wasted truth. The cause is a divine curse, not the hearers’ low quality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “As Heraclitus says ‘asses would prefer sweepings to gold’; for food is pleasanter than gold to asses.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle quotes Heraclitus to show that different kinds of creatures take pleasure in different things. The unfit cannot value what is precious.
philosophy.tie_back: Gold before asses is the Kural’s nectar before those not of one’s kind: worth that the audience cannot recognise.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.5 (trans. W. D. Ross), quoting Heraclitus (DK B9)
philosophy._accuracy_note: A vivid parallel of value lost on the wrong recipient. Aristotle uses it to make a point about pleasure, not speech.
